summary: Before Double 11, Chinese shoppers stock up on AI 'tokens'; AI-made short dramas flood screens; and a professor's death exposes pay-to-publish research quotas.
body: Ahead of Double 11 (Nov 11), China's biggest online sale, AI is being sold like a household good. Shoppers can buy packages of "tokens", the units of text an AI model processes, from Alibaba, MiniMax, Moonshot, DeepSeek and others on Tmall and JD.com, Reuters reports.[^1] Livestream star Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships for an Alibaba office AI tool in half an hour, Alibaba says.[^1] An analyst warned buyers may hesitate to prepay for services that could soon be replaced.[^1]

AI is also changing entertainment. China's TV and online video regulator says nearly 550,000 short dramas, series of episodes a minute or two long watched on phones, were released in the first ten months of 2026, about 17 times last year's number, Caixin reports; Caixin's summary says most were made with AI.[^3] Traditional TV makers are on the defensive.[^3] Separately, lidar, the laser sensors that help cars "see" in 3D, now appears on Chinese cars costing 60,000 to 80,000 yuan (about $11,000 to $15,000 CAD), as prices have fallen by about three-quarters in three years, the maker Hesai says.[^4]

Daily life: the death in October of Bai Baoguo, a music professor at Yan'an University, has drawn attention to research quotas. Caixin reports his final letter says he would have had to pay about 200,000 yuan of his own money to fund and publish research to keep his job, and other teachers describe similar "pay to work" pressure.[^5] Shaanxi's education department has set up an investigation; the claims have not been verified.[^5] China's October trade figures are due Nov 10.

reads.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
reads.summary: A young factory worker built a bedbug-reporting app with AI; it drew 300,000 users, then refund fights. A story about trust, apps and reviews.
